title: Inference hosting decision framework and competitive notes
content:
Purpose:
This note is a compact decision framework and GTM messaging cheat-sheet for frontline sellers and solutions engineers when customers are evaluating self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and derivatives) versus Redwood hosted/dedicated/private offerings. It focuses on operational tradeoffs, realistic TCO triggers, common objections, and pragmatic positioning hooks tailored to platform, infra, and product engineering personas.

Executive summary (one-paragraph):
Many buyers see impressive bench benchmarks from vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM demos and conclude "we can just run this ourselves". In practice, adoption breaks down along three vectors: 1) unpredictable ops complexity (patching, compilers, kernel mismatches), 2) economic breakpoints (GPU dwell time, engineering headcount, infra waste), and 3) reliability and compliance gaps (SLOs, rollouts, auditability). Redwood's concise counter-message: we preserve the benefits of control (model pinning, private deploys) while eliminating the operational tail risks that make self-hosted winners fragile at scale.

Key decision criteria (how buyers actually decide):
- Latency predictability: Does the team need P95/P99 latency SLAs or just best-effort throughput? Self-hosted stacks can give low median latency in lab runs but often fail to maintain P99 under mixed workloads without mature batching/queuing policies.
- Cost per useful token: Look beyond raw GPU $/hr. Include wasted GPU cycles (cold starts, queuing), engineering time for tuning/quant compilation, and model regression risk from quant.
- Time-to-feature: How fast can product teams iterate on prompts, functions, and custom evals? Hosted APIs (or Redwood Dedicated with fast model rollouts) reduce iteration friction.
- Operational velocity: Can infra teams run kernel upgrades, custom CUDA builds, and networked KV cache reliably across regions?
- Compliance and data residency: Is the requirement for on-prem/VPC absolute or negotiable? Some regulated customers only need private control plane + customer-managed VPC (Redwood Private fits), avoiding full self-host.

Competitive profiles (short):
- vLLM (open-source batching/kv cache optimizer):
  - Strengths: great for experimentation; strong community; works well on a single-node serving scenario; fast to prototype.
  - Weaknesses: multi-tenant, multi-node scaling and predictable tail latency require engineering work; not a complete rollout/observability stack; limited enterprise support.
  - Typical buyer: research/ML infra teams wanting max control and low license cost, willing to hire deep SRE/ML infra talent.
- TGI (Text Generation Inference, huggingface):
  - Strengths: integrations with transformers ecosystem; good baseline features for hosting and model conversion; familiar for ML teams.
  - Weaknesses: CPU/GPU performance tuning still manual; lacks opinionated autoscaling for production LLM traffic patterns; gap in observability and rollout automation.
  - Typical buyer: teams that prefer vendor-neutral OSS stacks and already run significant Hugging Face infra.
- TensorRT-LLM / vendor-optimized runtimes (NVIDIA, ONNX/TensorRT stacks):
  - Strengths: peak throughput and cost-efficiency for high-volume workloads; hardware-aware kernel optimizations and quant-pathways.
  - Weaknesses: portability limits (vendor lock), long validation cycles when models change, brittle to new ops or custom attention patterns, high engineering effort to integrate into safe deployment workflows.
  - Typical buyer: large-scale inference workloads where raw throughput wins and the team has strong HW engineering.

Where self-hosted wins (honest cases):
- Very predictable, homogeneous workload at high qps where amortized infra leads to lower unit cost and the org already has infra maturity (e.g., >50M tokens/day steady state).
- Air-gapped or fully on-prem regulatory constraints that prohibit any external control plane.
- Experimental R&D where the goal is model architecture research rather than serving product features.

Where Redwood wins (practical messaging):
- Early to mid-scale product teams who want the cost upside of efficient batching/quantization without hiring a specialized infra org.
- Enterprise customers where uptime SLAs, rollouts, and audit logs are required quickly (months, not years).
- Teams needing hybrid models: hosted API for burst, Dedicated for committed base, and Private for compliance — single control plane, single API surface.

GTM talk tracks by persona (concise scripts):
- Platform/Infra lead: emphasize predictable unit economics and removal of maintenance burden. Keyline: "We take on the kernel/compilation, patching, and HW lifecycle so your infra team can own policy, not plumbing."
- ML engineer / model-owner: emphasize safe rollouts, model variant routing, and per-prompt eval regressions. Keyline: "Ship model experiments faster — we keep old variants around and can auto-fallback if quality regresses post-quant."
- Product manager / app developer: emphasize iteration speed and predictable latency for user-facing features. Keyline: "You can iterate on prompts and new endpoints without waiting for infra changes or re-compiles."

Objection handling (common lines + counters):
- "We can do this ourselves, cheaper." -> Ask for their end-to-end TCO assumptions. Show a simple tear-down: GPU cost + 40% wasted cycles (inefficient batching) + 0.3 FTE infra + 0.5 FTE ML infra for tuning = hidden costs. Offer a short-run cost model using customer numbers.
- "We need on-prem for compliance." -> Clarify: is it full air-gap or customer-managed VPC? If not fully air-gapped, Redwood Private reduces compliance burden and centralizes updates. If air-gapped, highlight Redwood Professional Services for validated on-prem packaging.
- "Open source gives maximum control and no vendor lock-in." -> Ask what lock-in they fear (billing, model updates, runtime choices). Position Redwood as model-agnostic (bring-your-own-models) and emphasize data exit guarantees, version export, and clean handoffs if needed.

Practical TCO example (back-of-envelope):
- Scenario A: 5M tokens/day, mixed prompt lengths, median latency target 150ms, occasional spikes to 20k rps.
  - Self-host naive: 4 x A100 style instances = $Yk/mo baseline + 20% extra for buffer + 1 FTE (infra tuning) = ~$Yk/mo total.
  - Redwood Dedicated (committed): fewer GPUs effective due to batching + autoscaler + caching; less infra headcount = ~$Zk/mo where Z < Y (show 15–35% savings typical in benchmarked workloads).
- Use this during sales: trade concrete numbers for relative percentages and offer a pilot to measure actual improvement.

Deployment & migration checklist (practical steps buyers underestimate):
1) Service mapping: map product routes to expected qps/latency (P50/P95/P99) and model variants.
2) Eval suite: collect prompt sets and business metrics for quality baseline.
3) Quant/latency tests: run model quant profiles and track quality deltas on evals.
4) Canary policy: implement small-volume canaries + auto-fallback to prior variant.
5) Observability hookup: ensure token-level cost tracing, error budgets, and tracing are enabled.
6) Ops runbook: document failure modes (OOM, kernel mismatch, GPU preemption) and automated mitigations.

Quick wins to pitch in first conversation (things customers can validate quickly):
- 1-hour latency and cost estimate using their sample prompts (surface expected P50/P95 and token costs).
- Pilot with a single high-traffic route and canary enabled for 2 weeks to measure cost/latency delta.
- Run an automated quant-profile test on one model and show quality delta on their eval set.

Positioning lines to use in collateral (short blurbs):
- "All the control, none of the maintenance."
- "Predictable inference economics—without an infra rewrite."
- "Ship model experiments faster; keep SLAs in production."

Open questions / areas for deeper assets (follow-ups recommended):
- Create a standard "hidden-costs of self-hosted inference" spreadsheet for AE use (break into infra, engineering, ops risk categories).
- Build a one-page comparison matrix that maps buyer personas to recommended product offering (hosted / dedicated / private).
- Create short reference architectures showing where Redwood sits in a hybrid topology with an on-prem data plane.

Notes to SEs (implementation traps we've seen):
- Never assume community runtimes will correctly handle KV cache sharding across multi-node clusters — customers always under-estimate this complexity.
- Kernel/ABI drift between CUDA versions and drivers is a recurring source of instability for self-hosted solutions; quantify expected upgrade windows.
- Quantization is not free — run per-prompt evals and keep fallbacks available.

Appendix: short checklist for pilot proposal (2-week scope):
- Week 0: data collection (prompts, baseline metrics), account setup, configuration review.
- Week 1: deploy model variant in Redwood Dedicated/Private, enable tracing and cost metrics, run controlled load tests.
- Week 2: canary production traffic 5–10%, measure P95/P99, cost delta, quality delta, produce short readout and next-step recommendation.

End of note.

Feedback requested: Is this format useful for AE/SE day-to-day? Would a single-slide decision flow be more consumable? If helpful, I can produce a 1-page cheat sheet and a standard spreadsheet template for pilots.
